title: Events in Node.js
idea: An event is a named signal that something happened. You register a handler, also called a listener, and Node calls it each time the event fires.

analogy.text: A doorbell. You do not stand at the door waiting; you carry on with your day and answer when it rings.
analogy.breaks: Node answers one ring at a time; later rings wait their turn.

points: Objects announce events by name. A server emits `request`; `process` emits `exit`.
Register a handler once with `.on(name, handler)`; Node passes it the event's data.
Your code never waits in a loop; between events the thread stays free.
So one thread can serve many connections, each reacting only when its event fires.

items.label: Register
items.text: Your script calls `on` for each event, then `listen`. Setup ends.

items.label: Wait
items.text: The thread is free. The open server keeps Node running.

items.label: Event fires
items.text: A request arrives, so the server emits `request`.

items.label: Handler runs
items.text: Node calls your handler with `req` and `res`. It returns when done.

items.label: Wait again
items.text: The thread is free once more. The next request repeats steps 3 and 4.

code.title: A server's events
code.caption: Step through it, then press Run. Every `event:` line comes from a handler you registered. HTTP servers get their own chapter.

walk.text: Create a server. It is an event source: it emits events by name.
Register a `request` handler. It runs once per request and receives `req` and `res`.
Register a `close` handler. It runs after the server shuts down.
Register a `listening` handler. Its first line runs when the server is ready.
The server sends itself one request, waits for the reply, then closes.
Start listening on a free port. This fires `listening` and starts the chain.

pitfalls: Register handlers once, at startup; adding one per request makes listeners pile up.
Keep handlers short: a slow one holds the thread, so every other event waits.
Attach handlers before the event can fire; Node does not replay missed events.

quiz.why: `on` only registers the handler. It runs when `exit` fires, after the last line, so A prints first.

takeaway: Events turn waiting into reacting: register early, keep handlers short.

starters: How is an event different from a callback?
